evidence.title: Tsagaan Agui Cave (Bayankhongor, Gobi-Altai): 700–30 ka Desert Karst Shelter
evidence.dateBasis: ESR, OSL & 14C limestone cave strata
evidence.summary: High inside the Gobi-Altai foothills, Tsagaan Agui ('White Cave') preserves deep Middle-to-Upper Pleistocene limestone horizons spanning Levallois flakes, red-jasper scrapers, and early blades formed when wet interglacials sustained steppe rivers across the Gobi.
evidence.limits: Lower carbonate breccia ages span wide ESR/paleomagnetic error bars across Pleistocene climatic swings.

evidence.title: Chikhen Agui & Chikhen 2 Rock Shelters (Gobi-Altai, Mongolia): Late UP–Mesolithic Microblades
evidence.dateBasis: AMS 14C on ostrich eggshell & hearths
evidence.summary: Above seasonal desert springs in southern Bayankhongor, Chikhen Agui preserves stratified Upper Paleolithic and Epipaleolithic grass-lined bedding hearths, wedge-shaped microblade cores, and perforated ostrich-eggshell beads adapted to hyper-arid transitions.
evidence.limits: Eroded talus slopes compress early Holocene levels near the shelter mouth.

evidence.title: Flint Valley / Tsakhiurtyn Hondi (Southern Gobi): 20-km Jasper Paleolake Quarry
evidence.dateBasis: Geomorphic paleolake shoreline & Levallois-to-microblade sequence
evidence.summary: Across 20 km of red and yellow jasper outcrops bordering the Valley of the Lakes paleoshoreline between Arts Bogd and Gourvan Saikhan, surface knapping floors track millennia of Gobi Middle Paleolithic to microlithic quarry expeditions.
evidence.limits: Deflated desert-pavement surfaces merge multiple episodes onto single deflation lag horizons.

evidence.title: Bayanzag / Shabarakh-usu ('Flaming Cliffs', Ömnögovi): 8000–3000 BCE Gobi Oasis Foragers
evidence.dateBasis: Direct AMS 14C on dune-hearth organics & ceramics
evidence.summary: Beneath red Cretaceous sandstone bluffs made famous by Roy Chapman Andrews in 1922, relict wetland springs at Bayanzag yielded thousands of microlithic points, perforated ostrich-eggshell beads, net-impressed oasis pottery, and grinding stones from greener Mid-Holocene summers.
evidence.limits: Wind deflation shifts loose dune scatters; intact hearths remain localized near buried marsh clays.

evidence.title: Baga Gazaryn Chuluu Granite Massif (Middle Gobi, Dundgovi): Bronze Kurgans, Xiongnu Tombs & Monastery
evidence.dateBasis: Pedestrian survey, Xiongnu grave 14C & monastic ruins
evidence.summary: Granite canyons trapping spring water in the northern Gobi form a continuous 3,500-year sanctuary containing Bronze Age *khirigsuur* mounds, Iron Age Xiongnu shaft graves, Turkic rock carvings, and the 17th-century Delgeriin Choir Monastery.
evidence.limits: Long palimpsest of pastoral campsites leaves sparse stratified architecture outside stone cemeteries.

evidence.title: Khavtsgait & Bichigtiin Am Gobi Petroglyphs (Ömnögovi & Bayankhongor): Chariots, Bactrians & Ibex
evidence.dateBasis: Spoked-wheel chariot & script epigraphy
evidence.summary: Along dark patinated basalt gorges of Gurvan Saikhan and Bichigtiin Am, Gobi herders pecked two-wheeled Bronze Age chariots, Bactrian camel caravans, fighting bulls, Turkic runiform signs, and snow-leopard hunts across arid mountain passes.
evidence.limits: Desert-varnish cation dating offers wide uncertainty compared with Old Turkic runic inscriptions.

evidence.title: Yinshan (Mount Yin) Desert Petroglyphs (Western Inner Mongolia): >50,000 Pastoral Engravings
evidence.dateBasis: Style sequence, Chinese-Tangut inscriptions & Ulanqab surveys
evidence.summary: Stretching across dark cliffs separating the Ordos Loop from the Gobi plains, over 50,000 engravings in the Yinshan range illustrate steppe wildlife, wheeled wagons, Xiongnu animal-style art, horsemen, and Nestorian–Mongol crosses.
evidence.limits: Carvings accumulate across overlapping nomadic confederations without uniform stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Tamsagbulag (Dornod, Eastern Gobi–Steppe): 6000–4000 BCE Pit-House Village & Plows
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified hearth 14C & bone-blade hoes
evidence.summary: At the eastern steppe frontier bordering the Gobi, Tamsagbulag excavated rectangular semi-subterranean mud-and-timber dwellings containing microblade-inset bone sickles, stone plows, cattle remains, and early ceramic jars.
evidence.limits: Whether Tamsagbulag practiced nascent millet/cereal gardening or intensive wild harvesting remains under study.

evidence.title: Salawusu / Sjara-osso-gol (Ordos Desert, Inner Mongolia): ~60–35 ka Ordos Tooth & Paleofauna
evidence.dateBasis: OSL, U-series & fluvial terrace beds
evidence.summary: Discovered along a deep canyon carved into Mu Us / Ordos desert sands in 1922, Salawusu yielded the classic 'Ordos Tooth' hominin incisor, fossil femur fragments, micro-cores, and butchered *Bubalus* and gazelle bones.
evidence.limits: Reworked river sand layers historically mixed late-Pleistocene and post-LGM fossils prior to modern OSL control.

evidence.title: Juyan / Edsen-Gol Frontier Oasis (Ejin Gobi, Inner Mongolia): >30,000 Han Garrison Bamboo Slips
evidence.dateBasis: Explicit Han dynasty regnal calendar dates on slips
evidence.summary: Dry gravel terraces along the terminal Edsen-Gol oasis preserve Han Dynasty rammed-earth beacon towers, granaries, and over 30,000 dated wooden and bamboo administrative slips documenting frontier rations, caravan passports, and beacon-fire signals across the Gobi.
evidence.limits: Hyper-arid winds preserve wooden texts selectively in buried watchtower middens.

evidence.title: Khara-Khoto / Heishuicheng ('Black City', Ejin Gobi): 1032–1372 CE Tangut & Yuan Oasis Metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Tangut script manuscripts, Kozlov archive & Ming siege strata
evidence.summary: Surrounded today by drifting Gobi dunes, Tangut Western Xia garrison-city Khara-Khoto (described as Etzina by Marco Polo) housed thousand-scroll Tangut Buddhist libraries, mosque domes, paper money, and water canals before drying up after 1372 CE.
evidence.limits: 1909 Kozlov archive excavations dispersed manuscripts between St. Petersburg and Lanzhou.

evidence.title: Noyon Uul (Noin-Ula) & Gol Mod (Northern Mongolia): Xiongnu Imperial Silk-and-Lacquer Tombs
evidence.dateBasis: Inscribed Han 2 BCE lacquer cups & Xiongnu aristocratic shafts
evidence.summary: Deep 15-meter log-chamber tombs of Xiongnu *shanyu* elites at Noyon Uul and Gol Mod preserve permafrost felt carpets embroidered with griffins, Hellenistic-inspired woolen tapestries, gilded horse-chariot fittings, and dated Han imperial lacquer cups (2 BCE).
evidence.limits: 1st-century looting hit central burial chambers while sparing richly preserved perimeter trenches.

evidence.title: Erdene Zuu Monastery (Orkhon Valley, Mongolia): 1586 CE Oldest Surviving Buddhist Monastery in Mongolia
evidence.dateBasis: 1586 Abtai Sain Khan foundation & 108-stupa wall
evidence.summary: Constructed from cut granite blocks recycled directly from nearby ruins of Mongol imperial Karakorum beginning in 1586 CE, Erdene Zuu became Mongolia's first enduring Gelugpa Buddhist monastic city linking northern steppes to Lhasa.
evidence.limits: Only core Zuu sanctuaries survived 20th-century destruction before restoration.

evidence.title: Khamaryn Khiid & Ongiin Khiid (Dornogovi & Dundgovi): 17th–19th c. Gobi Monasteries & Learning Hubs
evidence.dateBasis: Monastic chronicles & ruined adobe-stone complexes
evidence.summary: Deep across the southern and middle Gobi, desert monastery complexes such as Ongiin Khiid (1660) along the Ongi River oasis and Danzanravjaa's Khamaryn Khiid (1820) functioned as libraries, medical schools, theater stages, and oasis caravan nodes until 1900.
evidence.limits: 1930s demolitions leveled most mud-brick temples; foundations and historical records document their 19th-century scale.

evidence.title: Yumenguan (Jade Gate) & Yangguan Passes (Dunhuang Gobi, Gansu): Han Great Wall Desert Gateway
evidence.dateBasis: Han Great Wall rammed-earth beacon towers & Dunhuang slips
evidence.summary: West of Dunhuang across howling Lop-Gobi salt flats, the square rammed-earth fort of Yumenguan (Xiaofangpan) and Han beacon walls controlled traffic leaving the Hexi Corridor toward Loulan and the Tarim oases.
evidence.limits: Shifting river oases drove periodic relocation of Tang-period customs stations farther east.

evidence.title: Jiaohe (Yarkhoto), Gaochang & Astana Tombs (Turpan Depression, Xinjiang): Ancient Desert Cities
evidence.dateBasis: Sunken-carved loess architecture & Tang-Uyghur texts
evidence.summary: Carved straight downward out of a loess mesa between desert rivers (Jiaohe) and built behind massive tamped-earth walls (Gaochang), these Turpan capitals preserve Christian, Manichaean, and Buddhist temples alongside Turfan Uyghur and Sogdian contracts from Astana's hyper-arid graves.
evidence.limits: Unfired adobe preservation owes to extreme rain-shadow aridity below sea level.

evidence.title: Xiaohe Cemetery & Loulan / Kroraina (Lop Desert, Xinjiang): Bronze-Age Mummies & ANE Genomes
evidence.dateBasis: Direct 14C & whole genomes on 13 Xiaohe mummies
evidence.summary: Desiccated by Lop Desert salt sands inside boat-shaped coffins topped by forest-like timber poles, the Bronze Age Xiaohe mummies revealed ancient DNA descended almost exclusively from local Ancient North Eurasians (rather than western steppe immigrants), thriving beside dairying and later Loulan Kharosthi Silk Road administrations.
evidence.limits: Extreme aridity preserved textiles, wheat, and kefir cheese while surrounding habitation settlements eroded away.

evidence.title: Kizil Thousand-Buddha Caves & Subashi Ruins (Kuqa, Tarim North Rim): Earliest Buddhist Grottoes in China
evidence.dateBasis: C14 wood/straw plaster & Tocharian B inscriptions
evidence.summary: Carved into Muzat River cliffs by Tokharian-speaking kingdoms of Kucha from the late 3rd century CE, 236 caves at Kizil preserve vivid lapis-blue Gandharan-Central Asian Jataka murals and central pillar stupas older than Mogao or Yungang.
evidence.limits: Radiocarbon dates on reed-tempered plaster refined art-historical periods back into the 3rd–4th centuries CE.

evidence.title: Dadiwan & Banpo (Gansu–Shaanxi Loess Rim): ~6000 BCE Broomcorn Millet & Yangshao Planned Villages
evidence.dateBasis: AMS 14C on charred millet grains & pig bones
evidence.summary: From earliest C4 millet cultivation and red-band painted tripod bowls at Dadiwan (~5800 BCE) through Banpo's circular moated Yangshao clan villages near Xi'an (~4800 BCE), interior northwestern river basins forged China's rain-fed millet agriculture and early concrete-like house floors.
evidence.limits: Early Phase I millet remains represent small-scale cultivation alongside foraging.

evidence.title: Majiayao & Qijia Corridors (Gansu–Hexi–Qinghai): Painted Spirals & Earliest East Asian Tin-Bronzes
evidence.dateBasis: AMS 14C & copper-tin-arsenic metallurgy
evidence.summary: Spanning upper Yellow River valleys from Lanzhou into the Hexi Corridor, Majiayao potters fired swirling polychrome urns while Qijia workshops cast a 2800–2000 BCE tin-bronze knife, copper mirrors, and horses/barley bridging Eurasian steppes and Central China.
evidence.limits: Exact direction of metallurgical innovations between Seima-Turbino/Hexi networks remains actively studied.

evidence.title: Jiahu (Wuyang, Central Henan): 7000–5700 BCE Playable Bone Flutes, Signs & Fermented Rice Beverage
evidence.dateBasis: AMS 14C on rice/flute strata & GC-MS residue analysis
evidence.summary: Excavations across 45 houses and 300 burials at Jiahu along the Huai headwaters uncovered the world's oldest intact playable red-crowned-crane bone flutes, chemical residues of fermented rice-honey-hawthorn wine inside pottery jars, domesticated rice and pigs, and incised tortoise-shell proto-symbols.
evidence.limits: Incised turtle-plastron signs are ritual marks ~5,000 years older than Anyang oracle bones, not a continuous deciphered script.

evidence.title: Chengtoushan & Shijiahe (Hunan & Hubei, Middle Yangtze): ~4500 BCE Walled Rice Metropolises
evidence.dateBasis: Moated earthworks, rice-paddy 14C & Daxi–Qujialing–Shijiahe strata
evidence.summary: Containing China's oldest known moated earthen city wall and preserved wet-rice paddies from ~4500 BCE at Chengtoushan, and later Shijiahe's 120-hectare citadel and jade-carving workshops in Hubei, the Middle Yangtze developed complex urbanism before Shang.
evidence.limits: Subsurface waterlogging preserves wood and paddies cleanly while flooding eroded upper residential levels.

evidence.title: Kuahuqiao & Hemudu (Lower Yangtze, Zhejiang): 6000–3300 BCE Stilt Houses, Lacquer & Dugout Canoes
evidence.dateBasis: Waterlogged timber 14C & lacquered bow/canoe
evidence.summary: Preserved in coastal Hangzhou Bay peat, Kuahuqiao (~6000 BCE, yielding the oldest East Asian dugout boat and lacquer-coated bow) and Hemudu (~5000 BCE, famous for mortise-and-tenon longhouses and thick domestic rice husks) showcase maritime timber engineering.
evidence.limits: Marine transgressions episodically inundated Kuahuqiao villages.

evidence.title: Taosi Walled City & Solar Observatory (Linfen, Shanxi): 2300–1900 BCE Pre-Dynastic Capital
evidence.dateBasis: 280-ha rampart 14C & 13-slot horizon alignment
evidence.summary: Sprawling across 280 hectares in southern Shanxi, Taosi combined royal tombs holding alligator-skin drums, copper bells, and flat-cast bronze gears with a semicircular rammed-earth pillar arc used to track sunrise solstices and seasonal calendars.
evidence.limits: Linking Taosi archaeologically to textual Xia/Yao traditions remains debated among archaeologists.

evidence.title: Shimao Monumental Stone Citadel (Shenmu, Northern Shaanxi): 2300–1800 BCE 400-ha Highland Polity
evidence.dateBasis: AMS 14C across East Gate & Huangchengtai palace
evidence.summary: Crowning arid Loess hills near the Ordos loop across 400 hectares of dressed stone fortifications, Shimao's colossal stepped Huangchengtai palace bore 70 carved stone relief monsters, over 4,000 jade insignia embedded into walls, horse-and-cattle herding, and bronze metallurgy.
evidence.limits: Vast monumental scale was unrecognized until major 2011–2018 excavations; peripheral towns remain under survey.

evidence.title: Sanxingdui & Jinsha (Chengdu Plain, Sichuan Basin): ~2500–800 BCE Bronze Masks, Ivory & Sunbirds
evidence.dateBasis: Pit-charcoal AMS 14C & Sacrificial Pits 1–8
evidence.summary: Isolated behind Himalayan foothills, the Ba-Shu Bronze Age civilizations of Sanxingdui and Jinsha buried thousands of elephants' tusks, life-size bronze figures, 3.9-meter sacred bronze trees, and paper-thin gold foil masks — utterly distinct in style from Yellow River Shang art.
evidence.limits: No deciphered written texts survive from Sanxingdui or Jinsha to name kings or ritual chants.

evidence.title: Dujiangyan Weir (256 BCE) & Mount Qingcheng Daoist Complex (Sichuan): Perpetual Gravity Irrigation
evidence.dateBasis: Qin bamboo/dynastic records & architectural chronology
evidence.summary: Built around 256 BCE by Governor Li Bing without damming the Min River, Dujiangyan's fish-mouth levee still splits floodwaters onto the fertile Chengdu Plain today beside Mount Qingcheng's 2nd-century CE Celestial Masters Daoist mountain temples.
evidence.limits: Levee stonework underwent annual bamboo-gabion maintenance over two millennia while temple pavilions date largely to Qing rebuilds.

evidence.title: Mawangdui Western Han Tombs (Changsha, Hunan): 168 BCE Silk Astronomical, Medical & Daoist Texts
evidence.dateBasis: Han dated funerary inventory slips (168 BCE Tomb 1/3)
evidence.summary: Sealed inside white kaolin clay and charcoal, Lady Xin Zhui's Tomb 1 and Tomb 3 (dated to 168 BCE) preserved her soft-tissue mummy intact alongside glossy lacquerware, the earliest complete texts of the *Yijing* and *Laozi*, planetary comets, and acupuncture-qigong silk charts.
evidence.limits: Preservation reflects exceptional kaolin-sealing of aristocratic tombs near the Xiang River.

evidence.title: Zuojiang Huashan Cliff Rock Art (Guangxi, South China): ~500 BCE–200 CE Luoyue Sacred Murals
evidence.dateBasis: Calcite U-series pigment bracketing & bronze-drum iconography
evidence.summary: High across 38 sheer limestone river cliffs along the Zuojiang–Mingjiang bends, ancient Luoyue artists painted thousands of towering red-ochre squatting dancers, horned chiefs, dogs, and Bronze-Age kettle drums facing turbulent river bends.
evidence.limits: Some painted scenes climb over 100 meters high where scaffolding methods remain reconstructed.

evidence.title: White Horse Temple (Baima Si, Luoyang, Henan): 68–1900 CE First Imperial Buddhist Monastery in China
evidence.dateBasis: Eastern Han imperial annals (*Hou Hanshu*) & Qiyun Pagoda
evidence.summary: Founded in 68 CE under Emperor Ming of Eastern Han to house Indian monks Kāśyapa Mātaṅga and Dharmaratna translating sutras brought on white horses along the Silk Road, White Horse Temple marks the institutional birth of Chinese monastic Buddhism.
evidence.limits: Standing halls reflect Ming–Qing rebuilds over a 12th-century Jin brick pagoda and buried Han–Tang precinct foundations.

evidence.title: Yungang Grottoes (Datong, Shanxi): 460–525 CE Northern Wei Imperial Cliff Monasteries
evidence.dateBasis: Northern Wei imperial inscriptions (Tanyao 5 Caves)
evidence.summary: Commissioned in 460 CE under Northern Wei Tuoba-Xianbei emperors across one kilometer of sandstone cliffs west of Pingcheng, 252 grottoes and 51,000 monumental Buddhas blend Gandharan drapery, steppe royal portraiture, and Chinese timber-facade replicas.
evidence.limits: Later Liao–Qing wooden facades shield exposed earlier sandstone carvings.

evidence.title: Longmen Grottoes (Luoyang, Henan): 493–1127 CE >100,000 Sandstone Cliff Buddhas
evidence.dateBasis: Dated dedicatory colophons (incl. 675 CE Fengxian Temple)
evidence.summary: Begun when the Northern Wei moved their capital to Luoyang in 493 CE and culminating in Empress Wu Zetian's monumental Fengxian Vairocana Buddha (672–675 CE), Longmen's 2,345 limestone caves trace 500 years of Chinese Buddhist and medical carving.
evidence.limits: 19th–early 20th-century head thefts damaged scores of minor niches prior to modern protection.

evidence.title: Maijishan & Bingling Temple Grottoes (Gansu Silk Road): 384–1300 CE Hanging Cliff Sanctuary
evidence.dateBasis: 420 CE Western Qin ink inscription (China's earliest dated grotto)
evidence.summary: Rising sheer along the Yellow River gorge (Bingling Si, holding China's oldest precisely dated 420 CE Buddhist cave mural) and the haystack peak of Maijishan, Gansu's mountain grottoes preserve fragile painted clay Buddhas accessible via stacked timber cliff walkways.
evidence.limits: Earthquakes along the Qinling fault collapsed central cliff ladders in medieval periods.

evidence.title: Shaolin Monastery & Songyue Pagoda (Mount Song, Henan): 495–1900 CE Chan Buddhism & 523 CE Brick Pagoda
evidence.dateBasis: 523 CE Songyue dodecagonal pagoda & Tang steles
evidence.summary: Founded in 495 CE in the Songshan central sacred range for Batuo and later Bodhidharma (traditional founder of Chan/Zen), the Dengfeng complex preserves China's oldest extant brick pagoda (Songyue, 523 CE), the Pagoda Forest, and Shaolin monastic chronicles.
evidence.limits: Rebuilt residential courtyards surround surviving Song, Jin, Yuan, Ming, and Qing brick stupas.

evidence.title: Mount Wutai: Nanchan (782 CE) & Foguang (857 CE) Temples (Shanxi): Oldest Surviving Tang Timber Halls
evidence.dateBasis: Original 782 CE & 857 CE beam ink inscriptions
evidence.summary: Sacred Mountain of Mañjuśrī drawing pilgrims from India, Japan (Ennin), Tibet, and Mongolia, Mount Wutai preserves China's two oldest standing wooden buildings — Nanchan Temple (782 CE) and Foguang Temple East Hall (857 CE) — rediscovered by Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin in 1937.
evidence.limits: Over 40 surviving monasteries on the plateau span Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing Gelugpa shrines.

evidence.title: Hanging Monastery / Xuankong Si (Mount Heng, Shanxi): 491–1900 CE Three-Religions Cliff Sanctuary
evidence.dateBasis: Northern Wei founding annals & Jin–Qing cantilever joinery
evidence.summary: Engineered into a sheer Jinlong Gorge cliff wall above Hunyuan in 491 CE, Xuankong Si suspends 40 timber pavilions on oak crossbeams mortised into solid bedrock, enshrining Śākyamuni, Confucius, and Laozi side-by-side.
evidence.limits: Exposed cantilever beam repairs in the 14th–19th centuries maintained the Northern Wei precipice layout.

evidence.title: Famen Temple Crypt & Giant Wild Goose Pagoda (Shaanxi): Xuanzang Translation Abbey & Tang Underground Vault
evidence.dateBasis: 652 CE pagoda inscriptions & 874 CE Famen crypt stone tablet
evidence.summary: Just west and south of Chang'an, Emperor Gaozong raised the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda in 652 CE for Xuanzang's Sanskrit translations, while Famen Temple sealed 2,499 Tang imperial gifts — Byzantine–Sasanian glass, gilded tea-service, and silk — inside a 21st-century rediscovered crypt closed in 874 CE.
evidence.limits: Wood-gallery interiors of the pagoda burned and were brick-reinforced in Ming renovations.

evidence.title: Leshan Giant Buddha (713–803 CE) & Mount Emei Monasteries (Sichuan): 71-m Cliff Colossus & Samantabhadra Peak
evidence.dateBasis: Tang 713–803 CE cliff-carving tablets & Wannian bronze hall
evidence.summary: Begun by monk Haitong in 713 CE to calm dangerous river whirlpools where the Min, Qingyi, and Dadu converge, the 71-meter carved stone Maitreya faces the sacred pilgrimage trails and Ming bronze halls of Mount Emei's summit monasteries.
evidence.limits: Earlier timber sheltering pavilions over the giant cliff Buddha decayed in late imperial times.

evidence.title: Dazu Rock Carvings (Chongqing): 650–1250 CE Cliff Sculptures of Three Traditions
evidence.dateBasis: Tang–Southern Song donor & sculptor inscriptions (Zhao Zhifeng)
evidence.summary: Hidden deep in the Sichuan–Chongqing hills around Beishan and Baodingshan, over 50,000 vividly polychromed Tang and Southern Song cliff sculptures synthesize Tantric Buddhism, Daoist immortals, filial piety tales, and everyday rural life.
evidence.limits: Seepage drainage networks carved inside Baodingshan rock face remain essential to pigment survival.

evidence.title: Wudang Mountains Ancient Daoist Temple Complex (Hubei): 7th–19th c. Imperial Palace-Monasteries
evidence.dateBasis: 1412 Yongle imperial construction edicts & Tang Five-Dragon shrine
evidence.summary: Stretching from Tang meditation caves through the Yongle Emperor's massive 1412–1424 imperial building campaign mobilizing 300,000 artisans across 33 complexes capped by the Golden Hall on Heavenly Pillar Peak, Wudang formed China's premier state Daoist mountain center.
evidence.limits: Many lowland valley palaces were submerged after the Danjiangkou reservoir damming beyond our 1900 horizon.

evidence.title: Labrang (Xiahe, 1709) & Kumbum / Ta'er (1583) Monasteries (Gansu–Qinghai Amdo): Monastic Towns of Tibet-China Rim
evidence.dateBasis: 1583 Kumbum & 1709 Labrang monastic founding annals
evidence.summary: Bordering the Tibetan Plateau, Loess Highlands, and Mongol steppes, Kumbum (birthplace of Tsongkhapa) and Labrang in Xiahe developed into vast six-college monastic universities teaching Tibetan, Mongolian, Han, and Tu/Monguor novices in medicine, debate, astronomy, and printing through 1900.
evidence.limits: 20th-century fires damaged several chanting halls later reconstructed on historic floorplans.

evidence.title: Chongsheng Temple Three Pagodas (Dali, Yunnan): 823–1900 CE Nanzhao & Dali Buddhist Capital
evidence.dateBasis: Nanzhao 823 CE Qianxun Pagoda core & 1978 relic chamber
evidence.summary: Rising beside Erhai Lake under the Cangshan peaks of the Nanzhao and Dali Kingdoms (8th–13th c.), the 69-meter brick Qianxun Pagoda (~823–859 CE) preserved intact gold-and-gilt Avalokiteshvara statues, Buddhist scrolls, and Nanzhao metalwork reflecting Southwestern Silk Road ties to Tibet and Myanmar.
evidence.limits: Surrounded outer wooden monastery halls burned in the 19th century while all three masonry pagodas survived earthquakes intact.

evidence.title: Qufu Temple of Confucius & Mount Tai (Shandong): 478 BCE–1900 CE Scholarly & Mountain Sanctuaries
evidence.dateBasis: Spring and Autumn records (478 BCE) & Han–Qing steles
evidence.summary: Consecrated over Confucius's residence in 478 BCE a year after his death and paired nearby with Mount Tai's imperial summit altars, the Temple, Cemetery, and Kong Mansion in Qufu conserve more than 2,000 imperial stone steles and Han-through-Qing ritual architecture.
evidence.limits: Standing timber pavilions reflect Ming–Qing imperial restorations around buried Zhou-to-Song foundations.
